strengths: The paper addresses an important question: why adversarial training can preserve clean generalization while leaving a substantial robust train–test gap.

Partial learning of shared signal combined with memorization of sample-specific noise is an interpretable proposed mechanism. Connecting representation complexity with training dynamics is a useful research direction.
The synthetic, MNIST, and CIFAR-10 experiments provide complementary observations, including model-capacity comparisons and measurements of the input loss landscape.
weaknesses: Theorem 4.4 is false under its stated assumptions. A balanced distribution on two sufficiently separated points can satisfy Assumptions 4.1–4.3, including having a vulnerable linear clean classifier. With N=D samples, both points have substantial empirical frequency with high probability; vanishing robust training error therefore forces zero robust test error, excluding CGRO. Additional distributional and sampling restrictions are necessary. Independently, Appendix F claims uniform o(1) approximation of the generally discontinuous memorization function by continuous ReLU networks, which is impossible without further qualifications.

Theorem 5.9 does not establish the claimed robust training guarantee. Definition 5.6 optimizes against perturbations restricted to the signal direction in the meaningful patch, whereas Definition 3.3 measures robustness over the entire norm ball. Small loss against the restricted attacks does not imply small full-ball robust training error. Appendix E.12 assumes this implication without proving it, undermining the conclusion that the trained network satisfies the stated CGRO definition.

The dynamics proof contains additional substantive errors. Lemma 5.11 effectively drops the factor 1−λ from the clean-signal contribution even though Assumption 5.7 permits λ=1. Appendix E.12 also incorrectly treats cubic Gaussian projections as sub-Gaussian when deriving vanishing clean test error; the stated concentration bound is invalid, and correlations across neurons sharing the same noise are not justified. These affect the central theorem rather than merely its presentation.

The supplementary generalization bound, Theorem B.1, is also unsupported as stated. A constant nonzero classifier has zero input gradient, making the proposed correction term zero, yet sampling fluctuations in class proportions produce a positive population-minus-empirical logistic-risk gap with probability approaching one half. A bound depending only on the displayed flatness quantity cannot provide the asserted high-probability guarantee.

The synthetic experiment uses δ=α=10, contradicting Assumption 5.7's strict δ<α. At this radius an admissible attack can erase the entire signal, leaving label-independent noise, so poor robust generalization can arise from information loss rather than the proposed learning mechanism. The real-data capacity sweeps and flatness correlations do not isolate that mechanism. Missing PGD step counts, step sizes, restarts, complete optimization settings, and variability across runs also limit reproducibility and confidence in the robustness measurements.

The originality of the claimed lower-bound extension needs clarification. Theorem 4.7 is existential over a broader distribution class, while Appendix F still constructs a linearly separable hard instance. This does not clearly establish a stronger result than the cited linearly separable setting of Li et al. (2022). Moreover, a worst-case representation lower bound does not by itself explain the behavior of the structured distribution or the image datasets. Given the failures in the principal guarantees, the promising framing and descriptive experiments are insufficient for acceptance.
